name: Find broken links and redirect chains across your site with Slack

parameters.content:
## Find the links on your site that are actually broken

A link checker is easy to write and hard to make useful. Most of what one reports is a host that refuses HEAD, a host that refuses robots, or a redirect that only adds a trailing slash. This checks each distinct link once and then judges what came back.

### How it works

The sitemap is read first - including the `<sitemapindex>` shape, where every `<loc>` is another sitemap rather than a page. **`Collect Every Link`** pulls every `<a href>` out of every page and **deduplicates by URL**, because the navigation is on all of them: a 40 page site produces about 2,000 links and a few hundred distinct ones.

Each distinct URL is fetched **once, with GET, without following redirects**. GET because `semrush.com` answers 405 to HEAD while serving 200 to GET. Without following, because the whole question about a redirect is where it goes.

**`Judge Every Link`** sorts the answers into four piles. *Broken* is 404, 410 and anything that refused to connect. *Blocked* is 403, 429 and 503 - `reddit.com` and `g2.com` answer 403 to any plain client, and calling that broken is what makes these reports unreadable. *Worth fixing* is a redirect whose target differs by more than a trailing slash, a scheme or a `www.` Everything else is fine. Only genuinely new problems reach Slack.

### Setup

1. Put your sitemap URL in **Settings**. Everything else there has a working default.

2. A Data Table called `link_rot` with columns `link_key`, `url`, `status`, `verdict`, `found_on` and `last_seen`.

3. A Slack credential.

4. `check_external` decides whether links to other sites are checked at all. Leaving it on is the point: your own pages rarely rot, the sites you linked to three years ago do.

## 1. Point it at your sitemap
Weekly, or by hand the day after a migration. Nothing here needs a key.

## 2. Two shapes of sitemap
`/sitemap.xml` is usually a `<sitemapindex>` whose entries are other sitemaps. Crawl those as pages and the run reads XML all day.

## 3. Follow the children
An index gets a second pass. A flat sitemap goes straight to the merge with its pages already in hand.

## 4. Every link, once
The navigation is on every page, so 2,000 links are a few hundred distinct ones. Relative hrefs are resolved by hand - the Code sandbox has no `URL`.

## 5. GET, and do not follow
GET because `semrush.com` answers 405 to HEAD. Unfollowed because the whole question about a redirect is where it goes.

## 6. Only what is new
A broken link stays broken. Reporting it every Monday until somebody fixes it is how the report gets muted.

## 7. The counts are the report
403 from a bot wall is not a broken link. Saying how many were ruled out is what makes the rest believable.

## Be polite to your own server

Both fetches are batched. Raising those numbers points a small crawler at your own origin, and your host will notice before your visitors do.
